## Follow the Energy {#sec-lay-ch01}

## A Concrete Picture

Imagine standing above a busy railway yard at dusk. A locomotive enters with
fuel in its tanks and motion in its wheels. It couples to a line of cars. Some
cars begin moving, one spring-loaded coupling compresses, brakes warm on another
car, and the last car eventually rolls faster than the first. If we watched only
the peak speed of each car, we would miss nearly everything that made the event
interesting. We would not know which engine supplied work, which coupling stored
energy for a moment, which brake removed it, or which force merely kept a car on
the curved track.

A golf swing is smaller and faster, but the accounting problem is similar. The
pelvis, trunk, arms, hands, shaft, and clubhead do not behave as a row of rigid
blocks passing a package along a conveyor. They are linked bodies whose geometry
changes while forces act. A connection can transmit power in either direction.
A segment can slow while still doing positive work on its neighbor. A large
force can redirect motion while transferring almost no energy. A flexible shaft
can accept energy, keep it briefly, and return some later. Gravity can help one
part of the path and oppose another. Damping quietly turns organized mechanical
energy into heat.

The first discipline of this book is therefore simple to state and surprisingly
hard to maintain: follow the complete energy ledger, not just the visible order
of speed peaks.

![A Five-Stage Map Connects Ground Contact, Body, Hands, Club, and Ball Without Treating Every Interaction as an Energy Supply.](figures/proximal_distal_companion/fig_companion_follow_energy.svg){#fig-lay-energy-route width=100% fig-alt="An interaction map links ground, body, hands, club, and ball; stationary ideal ground contact can redirect momentum without supplying work."}

The familiar phrase *proximal to distal* means, roughly, from nearer the center
of the body toward farther-away segments. In golf, researchers often describe a
sequence in which pelvis speed peaks, then trunk speed, then arm or hand speed,
and finally club speed. Ordered peaks have been reported, but the reported order depends on which
segments and angular-velocity quantities are measured [@tinmark2010; @marsan2019].
It is an observation about motion. It is not yet an explanation of energy flow. The explanation requires
forces, moments, velocities, and the boundaries across which power is computed.

## How the Mechanism Works

Begin with a modest definition. Mechanical energy is a bookkeeping quantity for
a chosen system. A moving rigid body has translational and rotational kinetic
energy. A raised body has gravitational potential energy. A bent shaft or
stretched tendon may have elastic potential energy. When external forces do
work, the system's mechanical energy can change. Internal interactions can redistribute mechanical energy, convert elastic
storage to kinetic energy, or dissipate mechanical energy into heat. Internal
muscles can convert chemical energy into mechanical work. Conservation of total
energy does not imply that the mechanical energy of a golfer-plus-club system
can increase only through external work.

That last sentence is the heart of the matter. Suppose we draw one boundary
around the golfer and club together. The forces between a hand and the grip are
internal to that combined system. The forces are equal and opposite. At an ideal shared no-slip contact their
material-point velocities agree, so the two contact powers cancel in the combined
ledger. If slip, deformation or an intervening compliant element is retained,
its power, storage and dissipation require explicit accounting. Merely reporting
the same physical contact in two ways cannot create an unexplained power gap. Now draw a smaller boundary around the club alone. The same hand
forces become external inputs to the club. They can change its kinetic energy,
bend its shaft, or redirect its motion. Neither boundary is more correct. They
answer different questions.

For a force $\mathbf F$ acting at a point moving with velocity $\mathbf v$, the
instantaneous power delivered through that point is

$$
P_F = \mathbf F \mathbin{\cdot} \mathbf v.
$$

For an applied free moment $\boldsymbol\tau$ acting on a rigid body with angular
velocity $\boldsymbol\omega$ in the chosen observer frame, moment power is

$$
P_\tau = \boldsymbol\tau \mathbin{\cdot} \boldsymbol\omega.
$$

For several forces on one rigid body, reduce their resultant force and moment
to one declared point. Pair the force with the rigid velocity field evaluated
at that point and the moment with the body's angular velocity.
The total power is the sum of the two terms; a moment arm must not be counted
again. A deforming club instead needs its contact/deformation velocities.
At a rotational joint, paired moment power uses relative angular velocity
between the bodies. Net joint power is not identified individual-muscle power.

These dot products are more informative than force or torque magnitude alone.
When force points generally with velocity, power is positive. When it points
against velocity, power is negative. When it points perpendicular to velocity,
it may bend the path strongly while doing no instantaneous work. A centripetal
force in uniform circular motion is the clean textbook example: it is essential
to the curved path, yet its dot product with tangential velocity is zero.

This gives us several distinct verbs for the swing. An actuator can **supply**
energy by positive work. An interaction can **transport** energy across a chosen
boundary. A spring can **store** and later **return** energy. Damping can
**dissipate** it. A perpendicular force can **redirect** motion. Constraint reactions can **redirect** motion or exchange power between
subsystems. A prescribed moving constraint can also supply external power; its
actuator must be included when the accounting boundary includes the mechanism
that moves it. Saying only
that energy “flows down the chain” compresses all those verbs into one and can
hide the mechanism we most need to understand.

Consider a relay race, another useful picture. The order in which runners reach
their top speed resembles a kinematic sequence. The baton resembles a physical
object crossing a boundary. But a golf swing has no single baton of energy.
Energy is a scalar assigned to states, and power is the rate at which work
crosses a chosen boundary. What passes through the wrist is not a glowing
substance. It is a calculable mechanical interaction whose sign and magnitude
depend on the force, moment, motion, reference point, and frame.

The technical study uses an energy ledger precisely because several mechanisms
can overlap. In a double-pendulum model, shoulder torque can add energy while
the arm-club interaction redistributes it. In the two-hand model, a pair of
opposed hand forces can create a club moment even when their net force is small.
In the flexible-shaft model, interface power can move into elastic storage and
return later. In an ideal stationary no-slip ground contact, reactions constrain motion
and provide impulse while doing zero boundary work. Deforming, slipping or
moving contacts require a different power calculation. The ledger asks each contribution
to identify itself rather than accepting one story for all of them.

### A Small Numerical Ledger

Suppose a simplified club receives $500$ watts of positive hand power for
$0.10$ seconds. If the power were constant, the hands would deliver $50$ joules
of work. During the same interval, imagine gravity contributes $3$ joules,
damping removes $5$ joules, and the shaft finishes with $8$ joules more elastic
energy than it began. Treat these as synthetic values and include all retained club kinetic modes
in $K$. Count gravity as external work here, rather than also including its
potential-energy change. The remaining increase in total kinetic energy is

$$
\Delta K = 50 + 3 - 5 - 8 = 40\ \text{J}.
$$

Nothing here says the shaft “lost” eight joules. At the chosen final time, those
joules are stored rather than expressed as total kinetic energy. If the shaft subsequently loses eight joules of storage, two are dissipated
and there is no other work or storage change, total kinetic energy rises by six
joules. This does not say that all six reach the clubhead. Timing and interface
powers decide which part holds the energy near impact.

![A Worked Energy Ledger Separates Hand Work, Gravity, Shaft Storage, Damping Loss, and the Remaining Kinetic-Energy Gain.](figures/proximal_distal_companion/fig_companion_energy_ledger.svg){#fig-lay-energy-ledger width=94% fig-alt="A bar chart balances fifty joules of hand work and three joules from gravity against eight joules stored in the shaft, five joules dissipated, and forty joules of total kinetic-energy gain."}

The same care is needed when a proximal segment slows. A slowing arm may be
losing kinetic energy, but that loss is not automatically equal to the club's
gain. The shoulder may still be doing work. Gravity and damping may contribute.
Interaction power may move energy between arm and club. Their kinetic energies
also depend on configuration because the inertia matrix of a linked system is
not a set of independent constants. The only safe claim comes from a closed
balance in a declared model or from measurements rich enough to estimate one.

**Model Result:** The [archived forward two-hand study](https://github.com/D-sorganization/UpstreamDrift/blob/a1a613999eb0c744da96caa040941955eb210a21/docs/research/proximal_distal_energy_transfer/data/forward_two_arm_study.json)
reports decreasing, nonzero work-energy residuals under timestep refinement.
Those numerical checks support bounded internal consistency, not exact
trajectories or biological validation. Chapter 29 distinguishes these residuals
from tighter algebraic wrench-power identities.

**Human Evidence:** Tinmark and colleagues reported ordered pelvis, torso and
hand peak angular-speed magnitudes in their 45-golfer study [@tinmark2010].
Marsan and colleagues found strong dependence of the identified sequence on
angular-velocity definition [@marsan2019]. These kinematic results do not measure
joint work or identify a causal energy-transfer route.

**Hypothesis:** A useful late-downswing strategy may depend on arranging the
state so passive and interaction terms assist the club while direct distal
actuation is delayed or even briefly opposing. The rest of the book makes this
proposal precise enough to challenge.

**Practical Interpretation:** Instead of asking which body part “creates all the
speed,” ask what each boundary is doing during each phase: supplying, carrying,
storing, returning, dissipating, or redirecting mechanical energy.

### A Swing-Phase Walkthrough

At address, the club already has a state and a preparation history. Its
gravitational potential energy is defined relative to a chosen reference height.
Raising it requires work against gravity; gravity has not supplied that positive
energy change. Holding a pose may require muscle activity even when the net
mechanical work is zero. Every later claim must name its ledger. During the backswing, muscles do
work to raise and rotate body segments and the club. Some of that work becomes
gravitational potential energy, some becomes kinetic energy, some is stored in
deformed tissue or the shaft, and some is dissipated. Saying that the backswing
“loads” the swing is therefore reasonable only after “load” is divided into
measurable forms.

Around transition, club speed may be low while forces and internal activity are
not. The direction of motion is changing, the golfer is reorganizing the state,
and compliant elements may carry load. This is a useful antidote to the idea
that low visible speed means nothing mechanical is happening. Early in the
downswing, proximal work can increase the energy of the whole system while the
club is still largely being carried. The club's own speed need not immediately
mirror the rate at which energy enters elsewhere.

In the middle and late downswing, the ledger becomes especially interesting.
For the whole club, hand power and gravity are external entries, while shaft
return is internal conversion from stored energy. Coupling to the body shapes
the hand power and trajectory; it is not a third external power to add to the
same ledger. At the same
time, one generalized torque can have negative power and still participate in a
state evolution that produces greater later club speed. Near impact, energy in
translation, rotation, and shaft deformation all affect the collision. After
impact, substantial energy remains in the body and club or is dissipated; the
ball never receives the entire pre-impact system energy.

### A Numerical Thought Experiment

Suppose two simulated swings both deliver a clubhead at 45 metres per second.
For a deliberately reduced example, represent each head as a point mass moving
at that speed: 0.20 kg in Swing A and 0.22 kg in Swing B. Their kinetic energies
are $\tfrac12mv^2=202.5$ J and 222.75 J. These are not whole-club energy estimates.
A rigid head requires center-of-mass speed and a separate rotational term; a
flexible club also carries distributed motion. Impact effective mass is a
directional contact-response property and must not be substituted for physical
mass in this energy calculation. Equal speed need not mean equal energy. Now suppose Swing A reaches that speed with 400 watts crossing an
interface for half a second, while Swing B has a 1,000-watt peak lasting only a
few hundredths of a second. The 200 J of interface work in Swing A is only one
ledger entry; initial energy, gravity, storage changes and losses must close
its complete balance. Peak power alone still does not say which boundary
supplied more work. Integrating the complete histories does.

The numbers are illustrative, not measurements of a golfer. Their job is to
force the vocabulary apart. Speed is a state variable, energy is a ledger
quantity, power is a rate, and work is an accumulation. When a result is
surprising, returning to those four definitions usually reveals whether the
surprise is physical or merely verbal.

### Questions for a Skeptical Reader

Before accepting any energy-transfer plot, ask whether all external powers were
included; whether the sign convention is stated; whether the shaft was modeled
as rigid or flexible; whether joint power was assigned consistently; and
whether numerical energy residuals are small relative to the reported effect.
Then ask the separate experimental questions: Were inertial parameters measured
or assumed? Were force and motion synchronized? Does uncertainty in those inputs
change the conclusion? A closed ledger earns the right to continue the
argument. It does not finish it.

## Where the Picture Breaks

Energy is not a liquid, electricity in a wire, traffic on a road, or a baton.
Those images help us remember conservation and boundaries, but they can mislead
us into imagining a material substance with a unique route. In a multibody
system, the decomposition itself depends on coordinates and system boundaries.
Some internal transfers can be described in more than one mathematically valid
way. Equivalent coordinate descriptions must recover the same physical motion and
consistent whole-system balance in the same observer frame. Moving to another
observer can change kinetic energy and power values without violating mechanics.
Individual coordinate-term labels are not invariant physical transfers.

The railway picture also makes couplings look sequential. In a swing, forces
act throughout the system at the same time. The distal club can influence the
proximal arms immediately through action-reaction. A shaft mode can affect grip
loads before its stored energy is returned. The correct picture is a coupled
network with time-varying geometry, not a one-way bucket brigade.

Finally, a closed simulated ledger is necessary but not sufficient. A wrong
model can conserve its own energy perfectly. Numerical closure shows that the
implemented equations agree with their accounting. Experimental agreement is a
separate question requiring measured motion, wrenches, shaft deformation,
ground reactions, and uncertainty.
